title: Denied hostname lookups reach the resolver because a Squid IP exception resolves names
symptoms: Resolver or DNS-policy logs show lookups for a hostname the agent was denied (TCP_DENIED / 403) in default mode
A hostname is refused by Squid but its name still appears in DNS telemetry
conditions: The generated squid.conf contains an API-proxy or explicit-IP destination exception (allow_api_proxy_ip or allow_ip_*) declared as dst without -n
The exception is evaluated before the domain deny, so Squid resolves the requested hostname to test it against the IP
Direct DNS queries from the agent, and lookups of allowlisted names, are outside this finding; they are governed by the trusted --dns-servers policy (NET-002)
rootCause: A Squid dst ACL without -n resolves a hostname destination before matching it against an IP, so evaluating the exception ahead of the domain deny issued a DNS query for an unlisted name even though HTTP access was then refused. dst -n matches literal IPs only, so a hostname is never resolved and does not inherit the IP exception. Only the API-proxy and explicit-IP http_access exceptions were verified; other dst ACLs were not reviewed for this finding.

probe.expect: Every matched ACL line carries -n (for example 'dst -n 172.30.0.30'). A line without -n indicates a build that predates the fix; no traffic is sent and no credentials or environment are read.

action: Use source containing numeric-only (dst -n) API-proxy and explicit-IP exceptions and regenerate the configuration. Keep the domain allowlist, raw-IP deny rules and rule ordering unchanged, and do not widen the allowlist or disable DNS filtering. This does not filter direct DNS queries or lookups of allowlisted names; use a policy-enforcing resolver through --dns-servers if those need control. If a denied name reaches the resolver with the fixed ACLs in place, escalate with redacted evidence under SEC-001 instead of reproducing it publicly.
